title: The three refuges
hookLine: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha: the three jewels people take refuge in

cards: When things fall apart, where do you go? A person you call. A place: a kitchen, a car, a bench.
A habit: the phone, the fridge, the bed at four in the afternoon. Everybody has somewhere they run to. Some of those places hold you.

Some just hide you for a while. Buddhism has a word for this, and a very old answer. It's the first thing a person says when they become a Buddhist, and it's said at the start of almost every Buddhist ceremony on earth.

teach.b: Tisarana. Ti: three. Sarana: shelter, a place of safety.
The three refuges, also called the three jewels: the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha. The Buddha is the one who woke up, and the proof that waking up is possible for a human being.
The dhamma is what he taught, and the way things actually are. The sangha is the community that practices it: in the oldest sense the monks and nuns, and more broadly everyone walking the path.
The Dhammapada knows the other kind of refuge well. In Max Muller's translation: "Men, driven by fear, go to many a refuge, to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees."
The verses go on to say those refuges don't end suffering, and point to the three jewels instead. Here is the formula, in Pali, unchanged for well over two thousand years. Buddham saranam gacchami.
Dhammam saranam gacchami. Sangham saranam gacchami. I go to the Buddha for refuge; to the dhamma; to the sangha.
It's said three times, with the words for a second time and a third time in front.

teach.h: THE FIRST TWO FOLLOWERS TOOK TWO.
teach.b: A lovely detail from the early texts: the very first lay followers, two merchants named Tapussa and Bhallika, met the Buddha just after his awakening and took refuge in only two jewels, because there was no sangha yet.
The third refuge arrived when the community did.
Refuge isn't a place you sit inside; it's a direction you keep walking in. For many Buddhists, saying it is a daily beginning, not a one-time membership card.

how: Buddhists recite the three refuges, usually three times in Pali or their own language, at the start of ceremonies, at home shrines and when formally becoming a lay follower.

o: three vows a monk takes on ordination day
going for shelter to Buddha, dhamma and sangha
three holy sites every Buddhist must visit

games.q: match the jewel to what it is.
p: what he taught; the way things are

s: the very first lay followers took refuge in all three jewels
Tapussa and Bhallika took two: there was no sangha yet.
sarana means shelter, a place of safety
the refuges are said once, when you join, and never again
they're said three times over, and many Buddhists say them daily.

games.q: you're a traveling merchant who meets the Buddha soon after his awakening. there are no monks or nuns yet. what refuge do you take?
o: the Buddha and the dhamma only.
none: you just give him food.
games.why: Tapussa and Bhallika went for refuge to the Buddha and the dhamma: two jewels, because the sangha didn't exist yet.

practice: Let the breath settle and, if it fits who you are, say the refuges quietly, the way Buddhists say them: Buddham saranam gacchami, Dhammam saranam gacchami, Sangham saranam gacchami.
If you'd rather simply listen, let the three words land one at a time: someone woke up; there is a way; others walk it too. Then rest in the breath, as if you had arrived somewhere safe.

wordCard.voice: Tisarana. The three refuges: the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, the three jewels Buddhists go to for shelter.

orig.note: Pali: the three refuges; sarana means shelter or protection.

carryVoice: Your line: three places to rest. Some places hold you; some just hide you. See you tomorrow.
